P3: I don’t know exactly how much of the future fear is accurate. AI may make human life enormously better, suck millions of people out of their jobs, end up between us and nearly everything as a sort of digital middleman, or do all three before Chantress Seba gets through her commune applications.
P4: Personally, I'd rather invest in more human independence than wait for certainty. It's better for me to have community and find out I didn't need an exit than to need an exit after spending ten years optimizing my feed.
P5: The useful question when you're designing a community is which connections to the technosphere you keep and which ones you limit.
P6: Medical care, banking, phones, vehicles, schools, supply chains, government ID, internet and energy are each a separate decision. If you opt out of them completely, it can cause needless suffering. If you depend on them completely, the outside system can reach directly into every essential function.
P7: The Amish, over generations, have made community decisions about where and if they want to use a piece of technology based on how it affects their community. Different Amish communities make different decisions. Some use it at work but restrict it at home. Some share it instead of everyone owning one. Others hold off on using it until they know more about its social effects. Whatever else you think of the Amish, they at least understand that adopting a technology is a decision for the group to make, and that it shouldn't get downloaded onto your device while you sleep.
P8: Medical care is one of the toughest connections to work out. A community may prefer natural care, but what happens if someone in the community needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dentistry, emergency obstetric care, or any number of specialist services? It is really important to decide in advance how people in the community are going to have access to care; what will be guaranteed with common resources; what may require money from outside sources (or insurance); and how the community will treat people who choose a different level of medical involvement.
P9: No member should have to jump through ideological hoops when they're scared or sick. If a community member becomes catastrophically ill, the community should already have agreed on how to support that person, including respecting their choices, making sure they have access to common resources or outside funds when it's needed, making sure they can get wherever they need to go, protecting their privacy, and allowing for the possibility that the community's preferred approach won't be enough.
P10: At the same time, social connection itself is measurably good for your health. The Surgeon General's advisory lists several health outcomes that isolated people are more at risk for. Community isn't a panacea, but it can make a difference, day to day, in the conditions people get sick, heal, age, and die in.
